Main Battery Energy Capacity (Wh).justification: Very high PI and 9,↑ link to office runtime justify a large battery for the professional model. Market references (XPS 15 ~86Wh, many 14–15" workstations 70–90Wh) show 80Wh is feasible without being extreme. Roof Matrix: higher Wh strongly increases battery mass and moderately increases system mass and thickness; we accept this to support heavy CPU/GPU loads where pros are often plugged in but still value long unplugged office work. 80Wh balances runtime with weight so that thermals and performance (CPU/GPU power) are still prioritized as required by the separation rationale.
Main Battery Energy Capacity (Wh).trade_off_notes: Accepts higher battery and chassis mass and slightly thicker base vs an ultra‑light design to avoid capping CPU/GPU power for battery reasons.

Standardized Office Battery Life Benchma.justification: PI is 0 for this PC, so it should not drive design decisions beyond ensuring basic competitiveness. With 80Wh and a professional platform (efficient 45–65W CPU class, dGPU mostly idle in office tests), ~9–12h PCMark 10 Modern Office at fixed brightness is realistic; targeting 10h keeps us on par with premium business laptops like ThinkPad T14s and many 14" pro notebooks without driving further trade-offs that might compromise thermals or performance.
Standardized Office Battery Life Benchma.trade_off_notes: Runtime is effectively a result of battery size and platform efficiency; we avoid chasing extreme 13–15h figures that would push us to reduce CPU/GPU power or screen brightness.

Battery Pack Mass (g).justification: Battery mass has mid‑high PI and is tightly coupled (0.9) to capacity. 80Wh packs in thin‑and‑light designs tend to be around 380–450g; 420g is a realistic mid‑point for a robust pro‑grade pack. This supports our 80Wh target while keeping total system mass reasonable given we also want strong cooling and structural rigidity.
Battery Pack Mass (g).trade_off_notes: Allows a somewhat heavier battery pack to sustain 80Wh, pushing overall system mass slightly above ultra‑portable competitors but aligning with professional expectations for runtime and performance.

Chassis Assembly Mass without Battery (g.justification: Chassis mass is PI‑moderate but central to durability, ports, and thermals (positive Roof links to drop height, casing durability, CPU/GPU power). With 420g battery, 980g chassis yields ~1.40kg system mass, consistent with high‑end 14" pro laptops (ThinkPad T14s ~1.3kg; sturdier/mobile workstations often 1.4–1.6kg). This higher chassis mass supports stronger structure, better cooling, and more ports/slots, matching this model’s professional positioning.
Chassis Assembly Mass without Battery (g.trade_off_notes: Accepts a heavier system than minimalist ultrabooks to gain durability, port selection, and cooling headroom, which also indirectly supports higher CPU/GPU power targets.

Closed-Lid Z-Stack Height of Display Mod.justification: Display module Z‑height has high PI and interacts with overall thickness, luminance, and reflectance. 4.0mm for the closed‑lid display module is slightly thicker than the absolute thinnest lids but leaves space for a stiff back cover, robust hinge anchor, and possibly higher‑brightness panel with proper diffusion layers. This supports a professional, durable lid without pushing total thickness too high.
Closed-Lid Z-Stack Height of Display Mod.trade_off_notes: Trades a few tenths of a mm vs ultra‑thin lids to improve panel rigidity and allow better anti‑glare layering and brightness uniformity.

Closed-Lid Z-Stack Height of Base Module.justification: Base Z‑height has the highest PI and is highly coupled to cooling, slots, and durability. A 15.0mm base (excluding feet) plus 4.0mm lid yields ~19mm closed thickness, similar to robust pro laptops (ThinkPad T‑series, many mobile workstations). This thickness enables stronger cooling (higher sustained CPU/GPU power), 2 SO‑DIMM slots, 2 SSD slots, structural stiffness, and FRU accessibility. It fits the separation decision favoring performance and serviceability over extreme thinness.
Closed-Lid Z-Stack Height of Base Module.trade_off_notes: Consciously sacrifices ultra‑thin aesthetics to gain cooling capacity, expandability, drop resistance, and FRU access.

Keyboard Switch Total Travel Distance (m.justification: Keyboard travel has high PI and a 9,↑ relationship to the key‑travel EC. Many business/pro laptops target 1.5–1.8mm; 1.8mm is on the higher‑comfort side while still compatible with a 15mm base height. This meets professional typing comfort expectations without excessively increasing thickness or conflicting with topcase stiffness.
Keyboard Switch Total Travel Distance (m.trade_off_notes: Slightly deeper than trend‑line 1.3–1.5mm ultrabook keyboards, but we accept the minor thickness pressure in favor of comfort and perceived quality.

Keyboard Switch Rated Endurance (million.justification: Endurance PI is significant; many premium keyboards rate 20–50M actuations. A 50M target (per key) signals pro‑grade durability for heavy typists. Roof Matrix shows a mild negative relation to casing surface durability, but that link is weak compared to the direct 9,↑ relationship between this PC and the endurance EC; modern switch designs can reach 50M without exotic materials.
Keyboard Switch Rated Endurance (million.trade_off_notes: Chooses a high lifecycle rating, accepting a marginal cost and potential design complexity increase for switches, but we do not push beyond 50M to avoid unnecessary cost and possible surface‑finish trade-offs.

Display Module Peak Luminance at Center.justification: Display brightness PI is high; pro users need legibility in bright offices and some outdoor use. Many 14–16" pro displays provide 400–500 nits. 500 nits at center balances usability, HDR‑adjacent headroom, and power draw. Roof Matrix notes negative correlation with battery and reflectance, but our 80Wh pack and strong anti‑glare mitigate this; 500 nits is a well‑established premium target in workstations and creator laptops.
Display Module Peak Luminance at Center.trade_off_notes: Accepts higher panel cost and some extra power consumption; compensated by large battery and focus on office workload efficiency rather than maximizing runtime under max brightness.

Display Surface Reflection Performance (.justification: Very high PI and 9,↑ link to surface reflectance EC. Premium pro displays often reach ~2–4% average reflectance with good matte/AR coatings. Targeting a ‘matte’ anti‑glare surface with ~3% reflectance ensures excellent usability under varied lighting, which also allows us to run at lower brightness in office workloads to preserve battery. Roof matrix shows slight trade-off with peak luminance, but 500 nits + 3% reflectance is realistic for current IPS or advanced LCD panels.
Display Surface Reflection Performance (.trade_off_notes: Slightly reduces apparent contrast/gloss compared to shiny panels and adds coating cost, but strongly improves legibility and reduces eye strain, aligning with pro priorities.

Display Active Area Diagonal (inches).justification: This model is framed as a professional laptop; 14" is a widely used sweet spot for mobility versus workspace in pro segments (ThinkPad T14s, many 14" EliteBook/X1 models). PI is one of the highest, and Roof Matrix shows strong influence on mass, thickness, battery, CPU/GPU power, and drop‑test. 14" keeps weight and size manageable while leaving room for serious cooling and ports in a 16:10 chassis.
Display Active Area Diagonal (inches).trade_off_notes: Forgoes 13" ultra portability and 15–16" expansive screens to strike a balanced, mainstream pro size compatible with strong thermals and acceptable weight.

Display Active Area Aspect Ratio (width:.justification: Aspect ratio PI is high; 16:10 has become the de‑facto standard for professional productivity (MacBook Pro, XPS, ThinkPad X1/ T). HOQ shows a 9,↑ relation to the aspect ratio EC; 16:10 improves vertical space for code, documents, and CAD UI vs 16:9 without excessively increasing lid height or impacting battery strongly. It’s also common in 14" pro panels at 1920×1200, 2560×1600, or 2880×1800 resolutions.
Display Active Area Aspect Ratio (width:.trade_off_notes: Slightly increases chassis height vs 16:9 but greatly improves usability for professional workflows.

SO-DIMM Memory Socket Count (sockets).justification: This PC has the highest PI of all; professional buyers and EC-10 place huge emphasis on memory capacity and upgradability. Two SO-DIMM slots are standard in 14–15" pro and gaming laptops and align with our thicker 15mm base. Roof Matrix indicates positive relations to mass, thickness, ports, and FRUs; we accept these to meet strong pro‑memory requirements and the Pro Graphics/Pro Cooling needs for future RAM upgrades.
SO-DIMM Memory Socket Count (sockets).trade_off_notes: Accepts some extra base thickness and board area vs single-channel/onboard configurations, and slightly higher power draw from dual sticks, but greatly improves capacity, flexibility, and repairability.

Maximum Supported Memory per SO-DIMM Soc.justification: High PI; EC-10 requires large max RAM capacity for professional workloads (VMs, CAD, AI). 32GB per slot with 2 slots yields 64GB max, a strong configuration common in modern SO-DIMM ecosystems without resorting to more expensive 48/64GB DIMMs. This balances cost with professional needs; 64GB total is adequate for most serious pro workflows for this generation.
Maximum Supported Memory per SO-DIMM Soc.trade_off_notes: Does not chase rare 48–64GB per DIMM capacities, which would raise BOM and potential timing/thermal complexity; 2×32GB remains mainstream and cost‑effective.

User-Accessible Internal Storage Slot/Ba.justification: Storage slot count has very high PI and 9,↑ link to the storage capacity EC and serviceable FRUs. Two M.2 NVMe slots (user-accessible) are common in performance‑oriented 14–16" laptops aimed at pros and creators. Roof Matrix shows trade-offs with battery, chassis mass, thickness, ports, and FRUs; with a 15mm base and 980g chassis we have room for 2 slots without critical sacrifices.
User-Accessible Internal Storage Slot/Ba.trade_off_notes: Takes on a small increase in mainboard area and thermal complexity vs a single-slot design to give professionals RAID options, scratch/project drive separation, and upgrade headroom.

Maximum Supported Capacity per User-Acce.justification: High PI; 4TB per M.2 slot is widely supported by current controllers and common in mobile workstations. With 2 slots, the system can reach 8TB total, matching or beating many pro laptops without requiring niche 8TB single drives. This fits the 9,↑ relation to storage capacity while respecting slot-count/capacity synergy in the Roof Matrix.
Maximum Supported Capacity per User-Acce.trade_off_notes: Avoids specifying bleeding-edge 8TB per slot, which would drive cost and compatibility/testing burdens; 4TB is mainstream high-end, balancing capacity and price.

Sustained CPU Package Power Limit at Key.justification: CPU sustained package power has very high PI and is critical for the Pro Cooling CR (9,↑ non-negotiable). Modern 14" pro/gaming designs with 15–19mm bases can sustain 45–60W CPU package power at acceptable surface temps. Targeting 55W at a 40°C keyboard surface is ambitious yet realistic given a 15mm base, ~1.4kg system, and dedicated pro‑oriented cooling. Roof Matrix shows this competes with battery life and thickness; for the professional model we deliberately bias toward performance, consistent with the separation decision that battery CR can at most modestly oppose CPU power.
Sustained CPU Package Power Limit at Key.trade_off_notes: Sacrifices some office‑work battery efficiency under sustained CPU load and tolerates a slightly bulkier cooling module to minimize throttling during heavy pro workloads.

GPU TGP as Configured (W).justification: GPU TGP has very high PI, strongly linked (9,↑) to 1080p gaming/graphics performance and co‑linked with CPU power in the EC/roof structure. For a 14" pro laptop with 15mm base and 80Wh battery, an 80W dGPU (e.g., mid‑range NVIDIA RTX class at 80W) is realistic and common; it delivers robust CAD/3D/AI and 1080p performance without overwhelming thermals or battery beyond what professionals accept (often used plugged in). This also leaves headroom for CPU power without forcing extreme dual‑fan, 2kg designs.
GPU TGP as Configured (W).trade_off_notes: Forgoes 100–130W GPU TGP found in thicker 15–16" gaming laptops to keep weight, noise, and base thickness within professional norms, while still far exceeding integrated‑only solutions.

1080p Gaming Performance Benchmark Score.justification: Gaming/graphics fps PI is high but somewhat below CPU/GPU power PCs. With an 80W modern GPU and 55W CPU, 120fps composite at 1080p low/medium across a fixed benchmark suite is an aggressive yet reasonable target, matching mid‑range gaming notebooks. HOQ shows this PC is primarily driven by GPU TGP (0.9 correlation) and somewhat by CPU power, consistent with the Pro Graphics CR; battery life is negatively correlated but our model explicitly prioritizes sustained performance for pros.
1080p Gaming Performance Benchmark Score.trade_off_notes: Higher fps implies higher GPU power and thus more fan noise and lower battery endurance during heavy use; this is accepted for the professional variant, consistent with the separation strategy.

Chassis Drop-Test Qualification Height (.justification: Drop-test PI is high. Many MIL-STD-810H‑rated laptops test around 1.22m (4 feet). Targeting 1.2m on a standardized test matches ruggedized business laptops while staying short of fully‑rugged ~1.5m+ designs. HOQ links higher drop height positively to chassis mass and casing durability; our 980g chassis and robust exterior are aligned with this requirement.
Chassis Drop-Test Qualification Height (.trade_off_notes: Accepts some additional mass and reinforcement in chassis and lid to achieve 1.2m rather than ~0.75–1.0m seen in lighter consumer designs.

External I/O Port Count by Type (weighte.justification: Port score PI is high and strongly tied to pro workflows (docks, monitors, peripherals). With a weighted score scheme, 18 units corresponds roughly to a rich mix (e.g., 2×Thunderbolt/USB‑C with DP+PD, 2–3×USB‑A, HDMI or DP, audio jack, SD reader, possibly Ethernet) similar to high‑end business laptops and mobile workstations. Roof Matrix positive relations with chassis mass and base thickness fit our already‑chosen 15mm base and 980g chassis.
External I/O Port Count by Type (weighte.trade_off_notes: Uses allocated chassis volume for a substantial physical I/O set rather than maximizing internal battery or marginally reducing thickness.

Casing Surface Durability Rating (standa.justification: Casing durability PI is very high; it also underpins drop-test performance. Many rugged business laptops advertise MIL‑STD‑810H compliance and coatings/hard anodizing around 7–9H pencil hardness. Specifying MIL-STD-810H environmental/drop qualification plus a 9H pencil hardness on critical surfaces gives strong scratch/abrasion resistance aligned with professional expectations and the HOQ’s 9,↑ link to finish wear resistance.
Casing Surface Durability Rating (standa.trade_off_notes: Higher finish hardness may slightly constrain keyboard switch design trade-offs and surface texture options, and can increase manufacturing cost; accepted to deliver a clearly professional durability level.

User-Removable / Replaceable FRU Count w.justification: User-replaceable FRU count has extremely high PI and strong 9,↑ relation to serviceable component coverage; the EC description lists RAM, SSD, battery, fans, hinges, Wi‑Fi card as the canonical six. Targeting all six as user-serviceable (no soldering) aligns this professional model with highly serviceable designs like Framework and some ThinkPad/Latitude lines. Roof Matrix shows mild negative interaction with battery capacity and system thickness, but our broader design already accepts a 15mm base and robust chassis, making this achievable.
User-Removable / Replaceable FRU Count w.trade_off_notes: Sacrifices some internal compactness and may add screws/covers, but supports pro priorities of longevity, repairability, and configurability; also differentiates the pro model from the casual sibling that might have fewer FRUs.

Main Battery Energy Capacity (Wh).justification: Very high PI and 9,↑ link to office runtime plus 0.5,↑ link to casual‑gaming runtime push toward a relatively large battery for this casual model. Mainstream 14–15" thin‑and‑light laptops with Ryzen 7 7840U‑class CPUs commonly ship with 54–75 Wh; 68 Wh is a strong but realistic capacity that still fits a non‑bulky chassis. Roof Matrix shows -0.9 conflict with CPU and GPU power limits, so we cannot simply maximize Wh; 68 Wh balances enabling ~8+ h PCMark office and >2 h capped‑fps casual gaming on battery while keeping pack mass and system weight acceptable for a casual user.
Main Battery Energy Capacity (Wh).trade_off_notes: Slightly heavier and thicker battery than a 50–57 Wh pack was accepted to support casual gaming and strong office runtime. In return, CPU and GPU power limits are set a bit more conservatively than in the professional_model to avoid runaway thermals and to honor the Battery×CPU/GPU 3,↓ efficiency relationship.

Standardized Office Battery Life Benchma.justification: Moderate PI but battery‑CR has 9,↑ importance on office runtime. Contemporary 60–70 Wh thin‑and‑lights at 15–28 W sustained draw in PCMark 10 Modern Office typically achieve 7–10 h; 8 h is competitive without requiring an oversized battery or very dim display. Roof Matrix shows 0.9,↑ with battery Wh and -0.9 with CPU/GPU power limits and -0.5 with display luminance and storage provision. We target 8 h by pairing 68 Wh with moderate 25–28 W sustained CPU power in office workloads and avoiding excessively bright or power‑hungry panels.
Standardized Office Battery Life Benchma.trade_off_notes: We forgo chasing 10–12 h ultrabook levels to keep enough CPU/GPU capability for casual gaming and responsive use. This lets us keep display brightness around 300 nits and maintain dual SSD support, accepting somewhat lower runtime than the most battery‑optimized ultrabooks.

Battery Pack Mass (g).justification: Battery pack mass has mid‑high PI. Market 60–70 Wh packs in 14–15" designs are typically ~250–320 g. Roof Matrix: strong 0.9,↑ with capacity and 0.9,↑ with system mass, plus -0.5 with CPU/GPU power. At 68 Wh, ~290 g is realistic using modern 21700/18650 or pouch cells without over‑engineering casing. This supports a sub‑1.5 kg target system mass when combined with a reasonably light chassis.
Battery Pack Mass (g).trade_off_notes: We allowed a heavier pack than a 50–55 Wh design to meet runtime goals, accepting a small penalty in system mass. In turn, this means we must keep the bare chassis and internals light to avoid exceeding typical casual‑laptop weight expectations.

Chassis Assembly Mass without Battery (g.justification: Highest PI among structural parts; strongly linked (0.9,↑) to base Z‑height, drop resistance, port count, and durability. For a 14–15" casual laptop targeting ~1.34–1.38 kg total mass (battery + chassis + small extras), a ~1.05 kg chassis without battery is realistic using aluminum/plastic hybrid construction. This mass supports adequate rigidity and drop performance while keeping the system portable.
Chassis Assembly Mass without Battery (g.trade_off_notes: We avoided ultra‑light <900 g chassis structures to maintain 1.0 m drop robustness, good port selection, and serviceability. The trade‑off is a system weight slightly above the lightest ultrabooks, which is acceptable for the casual segment in exchange for durability and expandability.

Closed-Lid Z-Stack Height of Display Mod.justification: Display module Z‑height influences overall system thickness (9, via EC‑3) but only has moderate PI. Modern 14–15" panels with slim bezels and metal lid assemblies typically reach ~4.5–5.5 mm. 5.0 mm allows a stiff enough lid for 1.0 m drop without resorting to heavy reinforcements and supports 300‑nit brightness while balancing reflectance control per Roof Matrix.
Closed-Lid Z-Stack Height of Display Mod.trade_off_notes: Slightly thicker lid than the thinnest designs was chosen to support durability and anti‑glare coatings. We give up a fraction of millimeter in closed thickness to avoid lid flex and panel damage failures common in ultra‑thin lids.

Closed-Lid Z-Stack Height of Base Module.justification: Base Z‑height has the highest PI and 9,↑ link to overall system thickness, keyboard travel, cooling robustness, and drop resistance. Casual users tolerate a slightly thicker machine if it improves keyboard feel and thermals. Mainstream casual laptops are commonly 17–20 mm closed; 17 mm offers space for 1.5 mm key travel, 2 SO‑DIMMs, dual M.2 slots, and a decent cooling module while not feeling bulky.
Closed-Lid Z-Stack Height of Base Module.trade_off_notes: We intentionally avoided ultra‑thin 14–15 mm bases to support better keyboard travel and cooling. This slightly increases thickness and mass but enables higher sustained CPU power and more ports, which are high‑TI ECs.

Keyboard Switch Total Travel Distance (m.justification: Keyboard travel has mid PI and 9,↑ link to key travel EC. Consumer laptops now often use 1.2–1.5 mm; 1.5 mm is strongly preferred by many users and still compatible with a 17 mm base height. Roof Matrix shows 0.9,↑ relation with base Z‑height and small positive links to cooling and durability. 1.5 mm balances a comfortable feel with chassis thinness.
Keyboard Switch Total Travel Distance (m.trade_off_notes: We sacrificed a marginally thinner base (e.g., 15–16 mm) to provide deeper travel. This supports perceived quality and comfort at slight cost to closed‑lid thickness.

Keyboard Switch Rated Endurance (million.justification: Keyboard endurance has moderate PI and 9,↑ link to its EC. Many laptop scissor switches are rated 10–30 million; premium office/gaming boards reach 50–100 million. 50 million actuations is a strong, realistic target aligning with mid‑to‑upper mainstream quality without requiring specialized mechanical switches.
Keyboard Switch Rated Endurance (million.trade_off_notes: We chose not to push to 70–100 million to avoid cost and travel compromises. 50 million is more than sufficient for casual usage patterns, freeing budget for battery and storage.

Display Module Peak Luminance at Center.justification: Display luminance has moderate PI and 9,↑ link to brightness EC, but higher brightness slightly harms office and gaming battery (-0.5 and -0.9). Around 250–300 nits is typical for mainstream IPS panels; 300 nits ensures usability in bright indoor and some outdoor shaded conditions. This level keeps power draw reasonable to protect battery metrics.
Display Module Peak Luminance at Center.trade_off_notes: We forgo 400+ nit premium panels to protect battery life and cost. That trades some outdoor readability for longer runtime and lower thermal load, appropriate for casual users who are more battery‑sensitive than brightness‑obsessed.

Display Surface Reflection Performance (.justification: Reflection performance has relatively high PI and 9,↑ link to reflectance EC. Many good matte laptop displays measure ~2–5% average reflectance; targeting a robust anti‑glare finish at 4% average reflectance is achievable while avoiding heavy haze that degrades image sharpness. Roof Matrix indicates this helps gaming‑on‑battery runtime and pairs well with moderate brightness.
Display Surface Reflection Performance (.trade_off_notes: We chose a strong matte finish instead of glossy/high‑luminance combinations. Some perceived contrast in very dark rooms is sacrificed in favor of better real‑world visibility and lower brightness requirements, reinforcing battery life.

Display Active Area Diagonal (inches).justification: Display size has high PI. For a casual‑use family sibling to a potential 14‑inch professional_model, 15.6" gives a larger, entertainment‑friendly canvas at modest added mass and power. The Roof Matrix shows 0.9,↑ links between diagonal and CPU/GPU power as well as slight negative impact on battery life. 15.6" is a widely available standard with good panel/mould availability and fits our weight goals.
Display Active Area Diagonal (inches).trade_off_notes: We accept somewhat higher power consumption and system mass than 14" designs to provide a more immersive casual‑gaming and media experience. This mandates a stronger battery and careful CPU/GPU power tuning to preserve runtimes.

Display Active Area Aspect Ratio (width:.justification: Aspect ratio PI is moderate. 16:10 is becoming the de‑facto standard for new 14–16" laptops, with good availability of 15.6"‑class or 15.3" 16:10 panels. It offers more vertical space for casual browsing and productivity without hurting gaming (slight -0.5 effect on gaming‑on‑battery runtime is minor). It also positively interacts in the Roof Matrix with battery and CPU/GPU tuning.
Display Active Area Aspect Ratio (width:.trade_off_notes: We avoid 16:9 to align with modern expectations, accepting a tiny penalty in gaming‑on‑battery efficiency for better general usability and differentiation from cheap models.

SO-DIMM Memory Socket Count (sockets).justification: SO‑DIMM socket count has the highest PI of all PCs, with 9,↑ relation to max memory EC and strong links to serviceability and I/O. Market backlash against soldered RAM is strong in reviews. Two SO‑DIMM slots is the standard for 14–15" chassis and enables dual‑channel performance and upgrades up to 64–96 GB with mainstream modules. Roof Matrix shows minor penalties to thickness and mass that our 17 mm base accommodates.
SO-DIMM Memory Socket Count (sockets).trade_off_notes: We accept a slightly thicker base and marginally higher board complexity to provide dual sockets. This sacrifices some ultra‑thin styling but strongly improves longevity, performance, and user satisfaction for both casual and pro buyers.

Maximum Supported Memory per SO-DIMM Soc.justification: Memory per socket has very high PI. 32 GB SO‑DIMMs are now mainstream and cost‑effective; 48/64 GB per slot remain niche/expensive. With two sockets, 64 GB maximum is more than enough for casual workloads and adequate even for many professional tasks. Roof Matrix shows minor impact on thickness and mass; 32 GB/socket is a sweet spot between capability and cost.
Maximum Supported Memory per SO-DIMM Soc.trade_off_notes: We deliberately do not target 48 or 64 GB per slot to avoid requiring higher‑density, pricier modules and PCB changes. This frees cost for better battery and storage, with negligible downside for the casual segment.

User-Accessible Internal Storage Slot/Ba.justification: User‑accessible storage slot count has very high PI and 9,↑ relation to max storage EC and serviceability. Two M.2 slots (e.g., 2x M.2 2280 NVMe) are common in 15.6" chassis and resonate with enthusiast expectations, enabling easy capacity upgrades and OS/data separation. Roof Matrix indicates small negative impact on office battery but benefits to serviceable coverage.
User-Accessible Internal Storage Slot/Ba.trade_off_notes: We accept minimal additional motherboard area and power leakage to support a second slot, trading a tiny runtime loss for major expandability wins and differentiation from budget single‑slot designs.

Maximum Supported Capacity per User-Acce.justification: Per‑slot capacity PI is high. 2 TB NVMe drives are now mainstream and affordable; 4 TB remains premium. Targeting 2 TB per slot (i.e., 4 TB max across two slots) aligns with TI for storage while keeping BOM cost moderate. Roof Matrix only weakly couples this to other PCs, so 2 TB/slot is a safe, market‑competitive value.
Maximum Supported Capacity per User-Acce.trade_off_notes: We avoid mandating 4 TB support (which may need firmware and validation effort) to contain validation cost and power variability. Users demanding extreme capacity are out of scope for this casual_model.

Sustained CPU Package Power Limit at Key.justification: Sustained CPU power at 40°C keyboard has very high PI and 9,↑ link to both thermal EC and gaming performance (via CPU‑bound titles). Casual Gaming CR demands a strong 9,↑ relationship but Battery CR imposes a 3,↓ efficiency link, and Roof Matrix shows -0.9 with battery Wh and runtimes. For a modern 7840U/Intel equivalent, 25–35 W is common; 28 W sustained under comfort‑limited 40°C keeps fans moderate, protects battery life, and still lets the integrated GPU reach good fps in casual titles.
Sustained CPU Package Power Limit at Key.trade_off_notes: We cap sustained power below 35–45 W pro‑oriented configurations, trading peak multi‑core performance for cooler surfaces, quieter operation, and better battery efficiency, which matches casual expectations.

GPU TGP as Configured (W).justification: GPU TGP PI is high and 9,↑ linked to 1080p gaming fps. For integrated graphics, effective package power is shared; we interpret this as effective sustained GPU allocation. Modern Radeon 780M/Intel Xe iGPUs at 25–30 W total SoC power can deliver 60+ fps at 1080p low in lighter/older titles. Roof Matrix shows strong -0.9 conflicts with battery runtime; 30 W is enough for “playable at modest settings” while still respecting efficiency expectations.
GPU TGP as Configured (W).trade_off_notes: We avoid discrete GPUs or 50–80 W TGPs that would devastate battery life. This trades away high‑end AAA performance but perfectly fits the P5.0 casual gaming brief and maintains portability and thermals.

1080p Gaming Performance Benchmark Score.justification: 1080p gaming performance PI is moderate–high; tied 9,↑ to GPU TGP and CPU power. For casual titles like Valorant, Minecraft, and GTA V at 1080p low/medium, integrated graphics at ~25–30 W can often sustain around or above 60 fps in many games per available benchmarks. A 60 fps composite target across a defined suite at standard low/medium settings ensures a responsive, console‑like experience without over‑specifying costly GPU hardware.
1080p Gaming Performance Benchmark Score.trade_off_notes: We do not chase 90–120 fps targets seen in dedicated gaming laptops, which would require much higher CPU/GPU power and a discrete GPU. This protects battery life, thermals, and cost while still hitting the casual “playable and smooth” bar.

Chassis Drop-Test Qualification Height (.justification: Drop qualification height PI is high. Rugged business laptops often advertise ~1.2 m MIL‑STD‑810H; mainstream consumer models typically are validated informally around 0.8–1.0 m. With a 1.05 kg chassis mass and 17 mm base height, engineering for a 1.0 m standardized drop is realistic and meaningfully better than minimal design practices, leveraging Roof Matrix’s 0.9 links between chassis mass, durability, and drop EC.
Chassis Drop-Test Qualification Height (.trade_off_notes: We chose not to pursue 1.2–1.5 m fully rugged standards to avoid structural weight and cost increases. 1.0 m is a practical compromise for casual users who want resilience to desk‑height drops without paying rugged‑laptop premiums.

External I/O Port Count by Type (weighte.justification: I/O port score PI is mid‑high and 9,↑ tied to its EC and to chassis mass. Interpreting weighted units roughly as: USB‑A=2, USB‑C DP+PD=3, HDMI/DP=3, audio jack=1, SD=2, Ethernet=3, a typical configuration of 2x USB‑A, 2x USB‑C (one with DP+PD), 1x HDMI, 1x audio jack, 1x microSD yields ~17–19 units. Targeting 18 supports good native connectivity for casual users (charging, external display, mouse, storage) without heavy docks.
External I/O Port Count by Type (weighte.trade_off_notes: We avoid extra specialized ports (full‑size SD, Ethernet) that would push thickness and cost. Users with more advanced needs can use USB‑C hubs, while casual users get strong baseline functionality.

Casing Surface Durability Rating (standa.justification: Surface durability PI is high with 9,↑ link to scratch/abrasion EC and 0.9 with drop height. Consumer laptops with anodized aluminum or hard‑coated plastic often test around HB–3H pencil hardness. Specifying at least 3H pencil hardness on outer surfaces (with HB base) strikes a balance: noticeably more scratch‑resistant than glossy plastic but not as costly as specialized coatings.
Casing Surface Durability Rating (standa.trade_off_notes: We do not target extreme anti‑scratch solutions that might degrade tactile feel or appearance. This slightly reduces resistance compared to premium ruggedized finishes but supports cost and aesthetic goals for the casual market.

User-Removable / Replaceable FRU Count w.justification: User‑removable FRU count PI is very high, with 9,↑ link to serviceability EC. The list: RAM (1 FRU), SSD(s) (1), battery (1), Wi‑Fi card (1), fans (1), hinges (1) could reach 6; however some hinges are better serviced at depot. Targeting 5 FRUs means RAM, at least one SSD, main battery, Wi‑Fi module, and fan assembly can be replaced with basic tools and no soldering. This honors strong user sentiment against non‑serviceable designs without over‑complicating mechanical design.
User-Removable / Replaceable FRU Count w.trade_off_notes: We accept slightly more screws, access doors, and internal cabling complexity (and minor mass) to reach 5 FRUs. We stop short of fully modular hinge or port boards to control cost and thickness.

Standardized Casual-Gaming-on-Battery Ru.justification: Casual‑gaming‑on‑battery runtime PI is moderate but directly carries the casual segment’s battery sensitivity and is 0.9,↑ linked to office runtime and negatively to CPU/GPU power and display brightness. Reviews show many gaming laptops deliver ~1–2 h; integrated‑graphics thin‑and‑lights can reach 2–3 h when frame‑rate‑capped. With 68 Wh and 28/30 W CPU/GPU limits plus 300‑nit panel, 2.5 h at a standardized capped‑fps 1080p low/medium workload is ambitious but realistic.
Standardized Casual-Gaming-on-Battery Ru.trade_off_notes: We do not chase >3 h gaming runtimes, which would require much lower power limits and fps caps, undermining the P5.0 gaming CR. Instead, we accept a mid‑range 2.5 h at enjoyable performance levels.

Sustained CPU Package Power Limit in Bal.justification: Balanced/battery‑mode CPU power in casual gaming has moderate PI and is 9,↑ coupled to main CPU power and 0.9 to gaming fps, but -0.9 to both office and gaming‑on‑battery runtime per Roof Matrix and 3,↓ preference in Battery×CPU relationship. On battery, many laptops significantly reduce CPU package limits to extend runtime and cap thermals; 20 W sustained during a standardized casual‑gaming workload maintains adequate CPU performance for the specified light/older titles while materially reducing battery drain versus 28 W plugged‑in limit.
Sustained CPU Package Power Limit in Bal.trade_off_notes: We purposely sacrifice some on‑battery FPS and CPU burst compared to AC operation to achieve the 2.5 h gaming‑on‑battery target and keep fan noise and skin temperatures comfortable, reflecting casual users’ battery sensitivity.
